topic: Idioms for Opinions, Work and Challenges

scenarios.scenario: Getting a project off the ground
scenarios.context: A team meets to launch a new app and agrees on a plan.

speakerA.en: Right, let's get the ball rolling. First of all, I want to make sure we're all on the same page about the deadline.
I know, but the client won't budge. If we cut corners, though, the quality will suffer.
That could save us weeks of work. Does anyone see a problem with that approach?
Fair point. Let's ask Sara. She knows it like the back of her hand.
While she checks, the rest of us can map out the main features and see how things stand.
Exactly. Let's meet again on Thursday and see where we are.

speakerB.en: As far as I know, we have six weeks, but that's a tall order given the size of the team.
Then we need to think outside the box. Why not reuse some code from our last app instead of starting from scratch?
Only one: the old code is a mess. Fixing it might mean going back to the drawing board.
Good idea. She's always willing to go the extra mile when we're in trouble.
Sounds good. I'd rather bite the bullet now than panic at the end.
Agreed. Let's hope everything goes smoothly.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether schools should ban mobile phones.

speakerA.en: Let me play devil's advocate for a moment. Wouldn't a ban simply push the problem underground?
Still, I tend to sit on the fence. Phones are distracting, but they can also be useful tools.
So where do you stand? Don't beat around the bush.
I don't see eye to eye with you entirely. Some teachers use apps in class, so a total ban in lessons would be unfair.
That's a decent solution. It would take a weight off the headteacher's shoulders.
I'm on board with that. Shall we write it up and present it to the student council?

speakerB.en: You've hit the nail on the head. Students would hide their phones instead of using them responsibly.
That's the elephant in the room. Nobody wants to admit that the same device can be both a help and a hindrance.
I'd allow phones at break times and ban them in lessons. That seems a happy medium.
Good point. Perhaps each teacher should have the final say, case by case.
It would. In the end, it comes down to trust: you can't force respect, only encourage it.
Why not? It's a long shot, but it's worth trying.

scenarios.context: Two employees talk after a hard week.

speakerA.en: I'm completely worn out. This week has been a roller coaster, and I haven't had a minute to myself.
The last straw was yesterday, when he asked me to redo the entire presentation an hour before the meeting.
I bit my tongue. I'm still learning the ropes, and I don't want to rock the boat.
Maybe, but the learning curve here is steep, and I don't want to make a bad impression.
Really? That's the first good news I've had all week.
Great idea. A break is just what I need to recharge my batteries.

speakerB.en: You and me both. I've been working under pressure ever since the new manager took over.
That's unreasonable. Did you say anything, or did you just grin and bear it?
I understand, but if you keep quiet, nothing will change. Sometimes you have to stick your neck out.
You're doing better than you think. People have noticed how you stayed late to help the whole team on the last project.
Trust me. Come on, let's grab a coffee and let off some steam.
My treat. After this week, you've earned it.

scenarios.context: A young couple discusses their finances before moving in together.

speakerA.en: Before we sign the lease, we should be honest about money. I'm barely making ends meet on my salary.
So we'd have to tighten our belts. No more eating out every weekend.
Good. And let's not break the bank on furniture. We can buy second-hand pieces.
Fair enough. What about our debts? Mine are only a drop in the ocean compared with yours.
We'll sort it out together. Once we're both earning more, we should be able to get back on our feet.
I agree. Money is a touchy subject, but it's better to lay our cards on the table now.

speakerB.en: Same here. Rent in this area costs an arm and a leg, and the bills keep going up.
That's fine with me. I'd rather save for a rainy day than splash out on things we don't need.
Agreed, although I'd like us to put a little aside for holidays. Otherwise we'll be tearing our hair out by the summer.
Thanks for reminding me. I'm still paying off my student loan, and it feels like a never-ending story.
I hope so. It's a relief to talk about all this openly, though.
Exactly. Honesty now will save us trouble later.

scenarios.context: A teacher talks to a student who failed an important exam.

speakerA.en: I was sorry to hear about your result. I know you were hoping for a better outcome.
That happens to the best of us. Remember that one bad day doesn't define you.
Not at all. You can retake the exam in the summer, and you'll be better prepared this time.
Absolutely. You've shown real talent all year, and the ball is in your court now.
That's the spirit. I'll give you some practice papers, and we can go over your mistakes together.
Sometimes a setback is exactly what we need to turn over a new leaf.

speakerB.en: I feel as if I've let everyone down. I studied for weeks, but my mind went blank during the exam.
I know, but it feels like the end of the world. All my plans have gone down the drain.
Do you really think I stand a chance? I don't want to get my hopes up.
It would mean extra work, but I'm ready to roll up my sleeves.
Thank you. I'd really appreciate it. Failing has been a wake-up call for me.
I'll remember that. Once I've passed, this will all be water under the bridge.
